text: You're on a night train that runs on rules. A man broke one and vanished. Then your phone rang, and it was your mom.
June pulls the phone from your ear and ends the call.
"Rule five," she says. "If someone calls your name, it isn't them."
Your hands won't stop shaking. "It sounded exactly like her."
"They always do." June picks her knitting back up, but her needles keep missing.
"How do you know all this?" you ask.
June is quiet for a long time. Then she holds up her ticket, punched so many times it looks like lace.
"November third, nineteen eighty seven. That was my stop."
"My mother was waiting on the platform, waving. Smiling too wide."
"So I stayed on." She looks down at her ticket. "I've stayed on ever since."
You look down at the rules sheet in your lap.
Rule six. Your stop is the one that shows your name on the map. Get off, no matter what is on the platform.
"June, the rules say you should have gotten off."
Her needles stop. She doesn't look at you.
Then you notice the handwriting.
The loops on the g's. The little line through the sevens.
It's your handwriting.
"I didn't write this," you whisper. "I've never seen this before."
In the black window, your reflection is still looking down at the page.
You're already looking up. It isn't.
Then your reflection lifts its head. And blinks.
You look away so fast your neck cracks.
"Rule eight," June whispers. "Good. Don't look back at it."
Above the doors, the route map flickers.
The name of the next stop scrambles, letter by letter.
Then it spells your name.
The brakes start to squeal. The train is slowing down.
June grabs your wrist. "Don't get off. Look at what's waiting."
The doors chime and slide open.
It's your mom, standing on the platform in her work coat, waving.
She is smiling. Too wide.
June's grip tightens. "It isn't her, sweetheart. It never is."
But the rules, in your handwriting, say get off, no matter what is on the platform.
Behind your mom, the platform lamp flickers off.
When it comes back on, she's one step closer to the doors.
